summary: This experimental memo adds digital signature authentication to OSPF link-state data and a certification mechanism for router data. It covers extra LSA processing, key management, and migration from or coexistence with standard OSPF version 2.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2154 describes digital signatures for Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing information. Routers can check who originated a link-state advertisement and whether it changed while being passed along.

questions: what is a router public key lsa
how does secure ospf authenticate lsas
what is a trusted entity in ospf
subtitle: An experimental extension that signs OSPF link-state advertisements.

tldr.problem: Neighbor authentication alone does not prove that routing information flooded across an OSPF network came unchanged from its originator.
tldr.mechanism: Routers sign their link-state advertisements, publish certified public keys in Router Public Key LSAs, and check advertised links against address ranges in the certificate.
tldr.outcome: The design adds end-to-end verification for signed LSAs but leaves incorrect claims by some routers possible. RFC 2154 is Experimental in the supplied metadata.

today: RFC 2154 is an Experimental memo published in June 1997, not an Internet standard. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Authenticating OSPF Routing Information
sections.content:
OSPF's simple-password authentication sends the password in cleartext. Keyed MD5 between neighboring routers protects local protocol packets, but the RFC says it does not authenticate routing data from its origin to its destination through the network.

This design signs each link-state advertisement (LSA) at its origin. The signature travels with the LSA, allowing receiving routers to check its integrity and origin after it has been flooded.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature lets a router check who created a link-state advertisement and whether its contents changed in transit. Neighbor authentication alone does not provide that check across the full flood path.

sections.title: Router Keys and Trusted Certificates
sections.content:
Each router signs LSAs with a private key and publishes its public key in a Router Public Key LSA (PKLSA). A Trusted Entity (TE) signs a certificate that binds a router identity, public key, role and permitted address ranges.

A receiving router verifies the TE's certificate and then checks the PKLSA with the router public key. The RFC does not specify how a TE is implemented or how it communicates with routers; TE public keys must be configured on routers that need to verify its certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: A router publishes its public key with a certificate signed by a Trusted Entity. Other routers check that certificate before using the key to verify the router's LSAs.

sections.title: Checking Signed LSAs
sections.content:
A signed LSA adds key identifiers, a signature length and a signature to an ordinary LSA. The first bit of its LS type marks the signature; a receiver stores an LSA only after verification succeeds and discards it after a failed check.

If the public key has not arrived, a router holds the LSA for the configurable MAX_TRANSIT_DELAY interval. For Router Links LSAs, it also checks that each advertised network link falls within an address range in the router's certified data.
sections.plainLanguage: A router checks an LSA's signature before using it for routing. It also checks that a router advertises only address ranges allowed by its certificate.

sections.title: Signed and Unsigned OSPF Areas
sections.content:
An autonomous system can contain signed areas and unsigned areas, but an area cannot contain both signed and unsigned LSAs. An area border router connecting the two types of area processes both and must not flood signed LSAs into unsigned areas or unsigned LSAs into signed areas.

This arrangement preserves routing connectivity, but the RFC says authentication and integrity apply only to routes inside signed areas or routes that pass only through signed areas. An ABR that is also an ASBR must use the same security configuration for all attached areas.
sections.plainLanguage: An OSPF network may connect signed areas to unsigned areas through an area border router. The signature protection applies only to routes that remain within signed areas.

sections.title: What Signatures Do Not Prevent
sections.content:
Signatures identify the router that originated information, but they cannot prove that the router's own claims are correct. An internal router may report a wrong metric or advertise a nonexistent host or stub network within its certified address ranges.

Area border routers can still originate incorrect summary information, and autonomous-system border routers can announce incorrect external routes. The RFC says ASBRs remain unprotected by this design and need other protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid signature proves which router made a claim, not that the claim is true. The RFC identifies incorrect information from internal and border routers as a remaining risk.
